paper.title: Assortative Mating and Education Gradients within and across Generations
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference are printed. …

registers.name_in_paper: the civil register (Danish Civil Registration System; Pedersen, 2011)
registers.role: sample frame and linkage: family quartets (two parents and their first two children)

registers.name_in_paper: the education register (Danish education registers; Jensen and Rasmussen, 2011)
registers.role: treatment: educational qualifications and years of education for all four family members

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (also called the income register; Baadsgaard and Quitzau, 2011)
registers.role: outcomes: annual labor earnings, disposable income, assets and wealth
source of annual pre-tax labor earnings reported by employers to the tax authorities
construction: imputed rent for owner-occupied housing in disposable income has been based on the property register since 1994

linkages: individuals linked across registers via unique personal identification numbers
family quartets (father, mother and the first two children) constructed as recorded in the civil register
each parent linked to their parish and year of birth to measure distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades
the source of middle-school locations is not named in the paper

sample.universe: all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018
sample.unit_of_observation: family quartet (father, mother and the two first-born children); the estimation matches correlations across family members, with child outcomes averaged over ages 31-45
selection_rules: all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018
children born between 1955 and 1973 (1955 is the first cohort with complete parent-child links; 1973 is the latest observed to age 45)
families with the two first-born children observed in this window: 122,532 families
families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables and outcomes
long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations per individual over ages 31-45
for the access analysis, families are split by whether the average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is below or above the median (40th / 60th percentile in Tables A2 / A3)
sample.n_observations: Table 1: 122,532 families; 243,564 children with education data; child-year observations 3,051,808 (labor earnings), 3,465,458 (disposable income), 3,465,663 (assets), 3,465,579 (wealth)
sample.n_individuals: 122,532 families of four members (122,532 fathers, 122,532 mothers and 245,064 children)

construction_notes: Years of education from the Ministry of Education's normed (shortest expected) durations; highest level taken from the qualification with the longest normed duration as of October 31 in the year the individual turns 29.
Annual pre-tax labor earnings: total annual earnings from all employment 1980-2018 from the Income Statistics Register.
Disposable income = personal gross income plus transfers minus taxes; footnote 2 lists revisions to the registered measure in 1984, 1990-1994, 1994 and 2002.

Assets = total non-pension assets at year-end (property, bank deposits, bonds, shares, mortgage deeds, cars, boats, cooperative apartment shares, business shares), excluding liabilities; 1980-1982 married couples' assets recorded under the husband are split equally between spouses; from 1983 assets, liabilities and capital income are split equally unless otherwise specified; 1987-1996 equity of self-employed businesses added; from 1997 asset measures rest almost exclusively on third-party reports.

Wealth = assets net of liabilities (total year-end debt including mortgage debt, bank loans, credit card debt, mortgage deeds in custody, student loans and debts to mortgage banks, finance companies, municipalities and other creditors).
Defined contribution pension plans are excluded for consistency over time (registered for the population only from 2012).
Monetary outcomes are in thousands of DKK at 2018 prices and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year.
Long-run outcomes: annual outcomes converted to annual percentiles, then averaged over ages 31-45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

Table 1 levels (thousand DKK, ages 31-45): labor earnings mean 385.7 (SD 233.4); disposable income 254.7 (205.2); assets 896.1 (1812.7); wealth 200.4 (1242.4). Years of education: fathers 11.9 (3.15), mothers 10.9 (3.12), children 13.4 (2.30).

Parental access to middle schools: distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, measured from the parent's parish and year of birth under the assumption that parents resided in their parish of birth until age 14; family-level measure is the average of the two parental distances.
Average years of education are 12.2 for fathers and 11.2 for mothers in higher-access families, versus 11.5 and 10.5 in lower-access families (footnote 12).

claims.statement: Jointly transmitted parental factors contribute 0.17 to the predicted own education–earnings correlation (σ_γδA).

treatment.label: Jointly transmitted parental factors (γ_A in education, δ_A in outcomes; parameter σ_γδA)

register_source.value: education register (for the education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (for the outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Latent factor capturing traits shared between parents which are jointly transmitted to their children — for example shared skills, resources or preferences, attitudes toward education, parenting styles or work ethic — the margin through which assortative mating can concentrate transmissible characteristics within families; σ_γδA is the correlation between its education and its outcome counterpart.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run labor earnings of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (income register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Annual pre-tax labor earnings from all employment, sourced from income tax returns via the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register, expressed in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: contribution to the predicted education–outcome correlation (correlation units; the model is estimated on correlations)

magnitude.interpretation: the joint parental component is large and statistically significant

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets with both parents born 1935–1954 and the two first-born children born 1955–1973
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: same-gender sibling pairs and mixed-gender sibling pairs (used to identify the sibling-shared component)

identification.source_of_variation: Covariance structure of education and long-run outcome percentile ranks across the four members of each family quartet (father, mother and the two first-born children); the sibling-shared component is identified from variation in sibling gender composition (same-gender versus mixed-gender pairs). No exogenous policy variation is used in the baseline model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

formal.as_written: s_Pj = γ_Aj + γ_Pj + μ_j + a_Pj  (1);  s_kj = γ_Aj + γ_Mj + γ_Fj + θ_j + a_kj  (2);  p_kj = δ_Aj + δ_Mj + δ_Fj + φ_j + b_kj  (3)

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; footnote 7 cites Bingley et al. (2021) showing that this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences.

implies_edges.from: Parentally transmitted factors (γ_A, γ_F, γ_M, δ_A, δ_F, δ_M)
implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

key_assumptions.assumption: Identifying normalization: the sibling-shared non-parental component σ_θφ is set to zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs, so that same-gender pairs identify the excess sibling-shared component; the paper states that the estimated parental transmission components should therefore be read as upper bounds.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A1 recalibrates the mixed-gender component to one-half of the same-gender estimate; the paper cites evidence that sibling spillovers and peer interactions are stronger within same-gender pairs (Dahl et al., 2024; Martin and Fabes, 2001).

formal.as_written: ρ^EO_CC = σ_γδA + σ_γδF + σ_γδM   (6')

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on families resident in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and the two first-born children born 1955–1973, and on children with at least five annual observations of the outcome over ages 31–45.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps are stated in Sections 2.1–2.2; the paper offers no assessment of how the conditioning affects the decomposition.

implies_edges.from: Family-quartet sample inclusion (two first-born children born 1955–1973; at least five annual outcome observations over ages 31–45)
implies_edges.to: Long-run labor earnings of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

threats_discussed: Mixed-gender siblings may also share non-parental influences relevant for education–outcome gradients, in which case the baseline normalization attributes those influences to parental transmission, so parental transmission components are upper bounds

Orthogonality of sibling-shared factors to parental transmission implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools; footnote 7 notes that Bingley et al. (2021) show this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences
robustness_checks: Table A1: the mixed-gender sibling-shared component is recalibrated to one-half of the corresponding same-gender estimate instead of zero
Tables A2 and A3: higher access redefined as average parental distance below the 40th and the 60th percentile of all parental distances
unresolved_confounders: Non-parental influences shared by mixed-gender siblings, which the baseline normalization attributes to parental transmission
Family sorting across neighborhoods or schools, which is ruled out by the orthogonality assumption
The decomposition does not identify the mechanisms behind the components directly

estimator.value: Equally Weighted Minimum Distance (EWMD), matching observed correlations in education and economic outcomes to their model-implied counterparts; standard errors corrected post-estimation using the inverse sample variances of the moments

estimation.specification: Latent-factor model of Equations (1)–(3) estimated on the moment system (4)–(7) by equally weighted minimum distance; σ_γδA is one of the five parameters of the education–outcome gradient system.
estimation.weights: equally weighted moments (identity weighting matrix); no sampling weights

sample_n.value: 122,532 families; Table 1 reports 3,051,808 child-year observations for earnings. Table 3 prints no N.

mediators_claimed: human capital, work-related preferences, and labor market orientation that assortative mating may align across spouses and that parents may reinforce jointly within the household (suggested; the paper states the decomposition does not identify these mechanisms directly)

ambiguities: The paper frames these quantities as correlations and decompositions of correlations, not as causal effects; the graph edge records the transmission channel the latent-factor model posits, not an effect the paper claims to have identified experimentally.

evidence.how: Table 3 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

Looked for a mean of the outcome in its own units: the outcome entering the gradients is an average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45, and no mean or standard deviation of that rank is printed anywhere. Table 1 reports the level outcome in thousands of 2018 DKK (mean 385.7, SD 233.4 for earnings), and the design has no control group or pre-period.

ρ^EO_FC = σ_γδA + σ_γδF,   (4)
ρ^EO_MC = σ_γδA + σ_γδM.   (5)

estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.

treatment.label: Mother's years of education

register_source.value: education register (qualifications recorded in the education register)

definition.value: Years of education, computed from the highest completed qualification recorded in the education register using the Ministry of Education's normed (shortest expected) durations; the highest level is determined from the qualification with the longest normed duration as of October 31 in the year the individual turns 29.

timing.value: Highest level of education as of October 31 in the year the mother turns 29; mothers born 1935–1954

outcome.label: Long-run assets of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: income register (Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Gross assets drawn from the income register, defined as the sum of financial and non-financial assets excluding liabilities (total non-pension assets at year-end), excluding defined contribution pension plans; in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: correlation (model-predicted gradient between the two percentile/education measures)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets with both parents born 1935–1954 and the two first-born children born 1955–1973
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). subgroups_defined: same-gender sibling pairs and mixed-gender sibling pairs (used to identify the sibling-shared component)

treatment.label: Mother's years of education

register_source.value: education register (qualifications recorded in the education register)

definition.value: Years of education, computed from the highest completed qualification recorded in the education register using the Ministry of Education's normed (shortest expected) durations; the highest level is determined from the qualification with the longest normed duration as of October 31 in the year the individual turns 29.

timing.value: Highest level of education as of October 31 in the year the mother turns 29; mothers born 1935–1954

outcome.label: Long-run wealth (net worth) of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: income register (Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Net worth, including both assets and liabilities (total year-end debt), excluding defined contribution pension plans; in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: correlation (model-predicted gradient between the two percentile/education measures)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets with both parents born 1935–1954 and the two first-born children born 1955–1973
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). subgroups_defined: same-gender sibling pairs and mixed-gender sibling pairs (used to identify the sibling-shared component)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Latent factor capturing attributes transmitted individually by the mother, for example personal abilities or behavioral traits that are not shared with the co-parent; σ_γδM is the correlation between its education and its outcome counterpart.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run labor earnings of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (income register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Annual pre-tax labor earnings from all employment, sourced from income tax returns via the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register, expressed in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets with both parents born 1935–1954 and the two first-born children born 1955–1973
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: same-gender sibling pairs and mixed-gender sibling pairs (used to identify the sibling-shared component)

identification.source_of_variation: Covariance structure of education and long-run outcome percentile ranks across the four members of each family quartet (father, mother and the two first-born children); the sibling-shared component is identified from variation in sibling gender composition (same-gender versus mixed-gender pairs). No exogenous policy variation is used in the baseline model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

formal.as_written: s_Pj = γ_Aj + γ_Pj + μ_j + a_Pj  (1);  s_kj = γ_Aj + γ_Mj + γ_Fj + θ_j + a_kj  (2);  p_kj = δ_Aj + δ_Mj + δ_Fj + φ_j + b_kj  (3)

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; footnote 7 cites Bingley et al. (2021) showing that this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences.

formal.as_written: ρ^EO_CC = σ_γδA + σ_γδF + σ_γδM   (6')

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

evidence.exhibit: Figure 3: Own Education–Outcome Gradient Decompositions by Parental Access to Middle School
evidence.annotation: Note: The figure presents the decomposition of predicted children's own education–outcome gradients in earnings, income, assets, and wealth into: (i) individual-specific factors, (ii) jointly transmitted parental factors, (iii) father-specific transmission, (iv) mother-specific transmission, and (v) non-parental shared influences within the family. The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. The average parental distance is computed by averaging the mother's and father's distances within the family. Higher-access families (High) are those whose average parental distance is below the median of all parental distances; lower-access families (Low) are those whose average parental distance is above that median. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.exhibit: Figure 3: Own Education–Outcome Gradient Decompositions by Parental Access to Middle School
evidence.annotation: Note: The figure presents the decomposition of predicted children's own education–outcome gradients in earnings, income, assets, and wealth into: (i) individual-specific factors, (ii) jointly transmitted parental factors, (iii) father-specific transmission, (iv) mother-specific transmission, and (v) non-parental shared influences within the family. The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. The average parental distance is computed by averaging the mother's and father's distances within the family. Higher-access families (High) are those whose average parental distance is below the median of all parental distances; lower-access families (Low) are those whose average parental distance is above that median. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.how: Table 5 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

Looked for a mean of the outcome in its own units: the outcome entering the gradients is an average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45, and no mean or standard deviation of that rank is printed anywhere. Table 1 reports the level outcome in thousands of 2018 DKK (mean 385.7, SD 233.4 for earnings), and the design has no control group or pre-period.

links.pointer_quote: We find that for assets and wealth, gradients in higher-access families contain a larger jointly transmitted component and smaller parent-specific components than gradients in lower-access families, whereas the composition of earnings and income gradients is largely invariant to parental educational opportunity.

claims.statement: Among higher-access families, jointly transmitted parental factors account for a proportion 0.47 of the predicted own education–earnings gradient.

treatment.label: Jointly transmitted parental factors (γ_A in education, δ_A in outcomes; parameter σ_γδA)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Latent factor capturing traits shared between parents which are jointly transmitted to their children — for example shared skills, resources or preferences, attitudes toward education, parenting styles or work ethic — the margin through which assortative mating can concentrate transmissible characteristics within families; σ_γδA is the correlation between its education and its outcome counterpart.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run labor earnings of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (income register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Annual pre-tax labor earnings from all employment, sourced from income tax returns via the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register, expressed in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets in higher-access families: those whose average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is below the median of all parental distances
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance to the nearest middle school at age 14 below the median of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above the median

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; footnote 7 cites Bingley et al. (2021) showing that this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences.

implies_edges.from: Parentally transmitted factors (γ_A, γ_F, γ_M, δ_A, δ_F, δ_M)
implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

key_assumptions.assumption: Identifying normalization: the sibling-shared non-parental component σ_θφ is set to zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs, so that same-gender pairs identify the excess sibling-shared component; the paper states that the estimated parental transmission components should therefore be read as upper bounds.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A1 recalibrates the mixed-gender component to one-half of the same-gender estimate; the paper cites evidence that sibling spillovers and peer interactions are stronger within same-gender pairs (Dahl et al., 2024; Martin and Fabes, 2001).

evidence.exhibit: Figure 3: Own Education–Outcome Gradient Decompositions by Parental Access to Middle School
evidence.annotation: Note: The figure presents the decomposition of predicted children's own education–outcome gradients in earnings, income, assets, and wealth into: (i) individual-specific factors, (ii) jointly transmitted parental factors, (iii) father-specific transmission, (iv) mother-specific transmission, and (v) non-parental shared influences within the family. The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. The average parental distance is computed by averaging the mother's and father's distances within the family. Higher-access families (High) are those whose average parental distance is below the median of all parental distances; lower-access families (Low) are those whose average parental distance is above that median. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.how: Table 5 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

Looked for a mean of the outcome in its own units: the outcome entering the gradients is an average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45, and no mean or standard deviation of that rank is printed anywhere. Table 1 reports the level outcome in thousands of 2018 DKK (mean 896.1, SD 1812.7 for assets), and the design has no control group or pre-period.

Significance read from the printed coefficient 0.27 and standard error 0.00 in Table 5: the standard error prints as 0.00, so it is at most 0.005 and the ratio is at least 54. The table prints no stars or p-values.

The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. The average parental distance is computed by averaging the mother's and father's distances within the family. Higher-access families (High) are those whose average parental distance is below the median of all parental distances; lower-access families (Low) are those whose average parental distance is above that median. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.how: Table 5 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

Looked for a mean of the outcome in its own units: the outcome entering the gradients is an average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45, and no mean or standard deviation of that rank is printed anywhere. Table 1 reports the level outcome in thousands of 2018 DKK (mean 200.4, SD 1242.4 for wealth), and the design has no control group or pre-period.

links.pointer_quote: We find that for assets and wealth, gradients in higher-access families contain a larger jointly transmitted component and smaller parent-specific components than gradients in lower-access families, whereas the composition of earnings and income gradients is largely invariant to parental educational opportunity.

claims.statement: Among higher-access families, jointly transmitted parental factors account for a proportion 0.50 of the predicted own education–wealth gradient.

treatment.label: Jointly transmitted parental factors (γ_A in education, δ_A in outcomes; parameter σ_γδA)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Latent factor capturing traits shared between parents which are jointly transmitted to their children — for example shared skills, resources or preferences, attitudes toward education, parenting styles or work ethic — the margin through which assortative mating can concentrate transmissible characteristics within families; σ_γδA is the correlation between its education and its outcome counterpart.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run wealth (net worth) of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: income register (Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Net worth, including both assets and liabilities (total year-end debt), excluding defined contribution pension plans; in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

magnitude.interpretation: jointly transmitted parental factors account for a large proportion of the gradient in higher-access families

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets in higher-access families: those whose average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is below the median of all parental distances
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance to the nearest middle school at age 14 below the median of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above the median

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; footnote 7 cites Bingley et al. (2021) showing that this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences.

implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

key_assumptions.assumption: Identifying normalization: the sibling-shared non-parental component σ_θφ is set to zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs, so that same-gender pairs identify the excess sibling-shared component; the paper states that the estimated parental transmission components should therefore be read as upper bounds.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A1 recalibrates the mixed-gender component to one-half of the same-gender estimate; the paper cites evidence that sibling spillovers and peer interactions are stronger within same-gender pairs (Dahl et al., 2024; Martin and Fabes, 2001).

key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps are stated in Sections 2.1–2.2; the paper offers no assessment of how the conditioning affects the decomposition.

implies_edges.from: Family-quartet sample inclusion (two first-born children born 1955–1973; at least five annual outcome observations over ages 31–45)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4.4 and repeated in the conclusion.

evidence.exhibit: Figure 3: Own Education–Outcome Gradient Decompositions by Parental Access to Middle School
evidence.annotation: Note: The figure presents the decomposition of predicted children's own education–outcome gradients in earnings, income, assets, and wealth into: (i) individual-specific factors, (ii) jointly transmitted parental factors, (iii) father-specific transmission, (iv) mother-specific transmission, and (v) non-parental shared influences within the family. The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. The average parental distance is computed by averaging the mother's and father's distances within the family. Higher-access families (High) are those whose average parental distance is below the median of all parental distances; lower-access families (Low) are those whose average parental distance is above that median. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.how: Table 5 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

Looked for a mean of the outcome in its own units: the outcome entering the gradients is an average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45, and no mean or standard deviation of that rank is printed anywhere. Table 1 reports the level outcome in thousands of 2018 DKK (mean 254.7, SD 205.2 for disposable income), and the design has no control group or pre-period.

Significance read from the printed coefficient 0.38 and standard error 0.00 in Table 5: the standard error prints as 0.00, so it is at most 0.005 and the ratio is at least 76. The table prints no stars or p-values.

The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. treatment.label: Jointly transmitted parental factors (γ_A in education, δ_A in outcomes; parameter σ_γδA)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Latent factor capturing traits shared between parents which are jointly transmitted to their children — for example shared skills, resources or preferences, attitudes toward education, parenting styles or work ethic — the margin through which assortative mating can concentrate transmissible characteristics within families; σ_γδA is the correlation between its education and its outcome counterpart.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run assets of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: income register (Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Gross assets drawn from the income register, defined as the sum of financial and non-financial assets excluding liabilities (total non-pension assets at year-end), excluding defined contribution pension plans; in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets in lower-access families: those whose average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is above the median of all parental distances
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance to the nearest middle school at age 14 below the median of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above the median

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.

implies_edges.from: Parentally transmitted factors (γ_A, γ_F, γ_M, δ_A, δ_F, δ_M)
implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

evidence.exhibit: Figure 3: Own Education–Outcome Gradient Decompositions by Parental Access to Middle School
evidence.annotation: Note: The figure presents the decomposition of predicted children's own education–outcome gradients in earnings, income, assets, and wealth into: (i) individual-specific factors, (ii) jointly transmitted parental factors, (iii) father-specific transmission, (iv) mother-specific transmission, and (v) non-parental shared influences within the family. The figure splits the sample by parental access to middle schools. For each parent, access is measured by distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades. The average parental distance is computed by averaging the mother's and father's distances within the family. Higher-access families (High) are those whose average parental distance is below the median of all parental distances; lower-access families (Low) are those whose average parental distance is above that median. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.how: Table 5 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

Looked for a mean of the outcome in its own units: the outcome entering the gradients is an average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45, and no mean or standard deviation of that rank is printed anywhere. Table 1 reports the level outcome in thousands of 2018 DKK (mean 896.1, SD 1812.7 for assets), and the design has no control group or pre-period.
Significance read from the printed coefficient -0.01 and standard error 0.03 in Table 5: the ratio of the two is 0.3, above 1.96. The table prints no stars or p-values.

evidence.exhibit: Figure 3: Own Education–Outcome Gradient Decompositions by Parental Access to Middle School
evidence.annotation: Note: The figure presents the decomposition of predicted children's own education–outcome gradients in earnings, income, assets, and wealth into: (i) individual-specific factors, (ii) jointly transmitted parental factors, (iii) father-specific transmission, (iv) mother-specific transmission, and (v) non-parental shared influences within the family. Levels, proportions, and standard errors are reported in Table 5.

evidence.how: Table 5 prints a coefficient and a standard error for each outcome and no p-values, confidence intervals or significance stars; no confidence level is stated.

anchor_quote.text: Higher-access families are those whose average parental distance is below the 40th percentile of all parental distances; lower-access families are those whose average parental distance is above that threshold.

claims.statement: Among lower-access families, individual-specific factors account for a proportion 0.45 of the predicted own education–earnings gradient.

treatment.label: Individual-specific factors correlated with education (a in education, b in outcomes; parameter σ_ab)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Child-specific factors, including individual ability and idiosyncratic shocks, that are neither shared within the family nor transmitted by parents; σ_ab is the correlation between the idiosyncratic component of education and the idiosyncratic component of the long-run outcome, identified as the residual component unique to the own education–outcome correlation.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run labor earnings of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (income register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Annual pre-tax labor earnings from all employment, sourced from income tax returns via the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register, expressed in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets in lower-access families: those whose average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is above the 40th percentile of all parental distances
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance below the 40th percentile of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above that threshold

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.

implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

definition.value: Disposable income, calculated as personal gross income plus transfers minus taxes, from the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register, in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance below the 60th percentile of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above that threshold

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; footnote 7 cites Bingley et al. (2021) showing that this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences.

implies_edges.from: Parentally transmitted factors (γ_A, γ_F, γ_M, δ_A, δ_F, δ_M)
implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

key_assumptions.assumption: Identifying normalization: the sibling-shared non-parental component σ_θφ is set to zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs, so that same-gender pairs identify the excess sibling-shared component; the paper states that the estimated parental transmission components should therefore be read as upper bounds.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A1 recalibrates the mixed-gender component to one-half of the same-gender estimate; the paper cites evidence that sibling spillovers and peer interactions are stronger within same-gender pairs (Dahl et al., 2024; Martin and Fabes, 2001).

anchor_quote.text: Higher-access families are those whose average parental distance is below the 60th percentile of all parental distances; lower-access families are those whose average parental distance is above that threshold.

claims.statement: Among higher-access families, individual-specific factors account for a proportion 0.39 of the predicted own education–assets gradient.

treatment.label: Individual-specific factors correlated with education (a in education, b in outcomes; parameter σ_ab)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Child-specific factors, including individual ability and idiosyncratic shocks, that are neither shared within the family nor transmitted by parents; σ_ab is the correlation between the idiosyncratic component of education and the idiosyncratic component of the long-run outcome, identified as the residual component unique to the own education–outcome correlation.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run assets of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: income register (Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Gross assets drawn from the income register, defined as the sum of financial and non-financial assets excluding liabilities (total non-pension assets at year-end), excluding defined contribution pension plans; in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets in higher-access families: those whose average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is below the 60th percentile of all parental distances
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance below the 60th percentile of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above that threshold

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.

implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

anchor_quote.text: Higher-access families are those whose average parental distance is below the 60th percentile of all parental distances; lower-access families are those whose average parental distance is above that threshold.

claims.statement: Among lower-access families, sibling-shared non-parental factors account for a proportion 0.08 of the predicted own education–disposable income gradient.

treatment.label: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ in education, φ in outcomes; parameter σ_θφ)

register_source.value: education register (education components) and the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (outcome components); the factors themselves are latent and not observed in any register

definition.value: Latent factor capturing sibling-shared environmental influences independent of parental factors, such as common school or neighborhood environments; σ_θφ is the correlation between its education and its outcome counterpart, identified from the excess environmental similarity of same-gender sibling pairs relative to mixed-gender pairs.

timing.value: latent family- and individual-level factors, time-invariant by construction; education measured at age 29 and outcomes over ages 31–45

outcome.label: Long-run disposable income of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register (income register); the paper names no register variable

definition.value: Disposable income, calculated as personal gross income plus transfers minus taxes, from the Statistics Denmark Income Statistics Register, in thousands of 2018 DKK and winsorized at the top and bottom 0.5 percent by year; converted into annual percentiles and averaged over ages 31–45, requiring at least five annual observations per individual.

timing.value: average of annual percentile ranks over the child's ages 31–45, observed 1980–2018

units.value: proportion of the predicted gradient (share of the correlation; the five/four shares sum to one)

estimand.target_population: Danish family quartets in lower-access families: those whose average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is above the 60th percentile of all parental distances
estimand.time_horizon: long-run outcomes measured as the average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

population.description: Danish family quartets — father, mother and the two first-born children — from all families residing in Denmark between 1980 and 2018 in which both parents were born 1935–1954 and the children were born 1955–1973; 122,532 families.
population.ages: children's long-run outcomes measured over ages 31–45; education measured at age 29
population.selection: All families residing in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and children born 1955–1973; the two first-born children must be observed in this window (122,532 families). Families with incomplete education or child-outcome information are retained, so the number of observations differs across variables; long-run outcomes require at least five annual observations over ages 31–45.
subgroups_defined: higher-access families: average parental distance below the 60th percentile of all parental distances
lower-access families: average parental distance above that threshold

identification.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: Education in each generation and the child's long-run outcome percentile are each the sum of orthogonal, zero-mean latent components entering with unit loadings (Equations (1)–(3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the model; the paper prints Equations (1)–(3) and offers no test of the factor structure.

formal.as_written: s_Pj = γ_Aj + γ_Pj + μ_j + a_Pj  (1);  s_kj = γ_Aj + γ_Mj + γ_Fj + θ_j + a_kj  (2);  p_kj = δ_Aj + δ_Mj + δ_Fj + φ_j + b_kj  (3)

key_assumptions.assumption: The latent factors are orthogonal within each equation, while cross-equation correlations between similar components (σ_γδA, σ_γδF, σ_γδM, σ_θφ, σ_ab) are allowed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.3; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sibling-shared non-parental factors are orthogonal to the factors transmitted by parents, which the paper states implies no family sorting across neighborhoods or schools.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; footnote 7 cites Bingley et al. (2021) showing that this restriction may overstate the role of sibling-shared influences.

implies_edges.from: Parentally transmitted factors (γ_A, γ_F, γ_M, δ_A, δ_F, δ_M)
implies_edges.to: Sibling-shared non-parental factors (θ, φ)

key_assumptions.assumption: Identifying normalization: the sibling-shared non-parental component σ_θφ is set to zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs, so that same-gender pairs identify the excess sibling-shared component; the paper states that the estimated parental transmission components should therefore be read as upper bounds.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A1 recalibrates the mixed-gender component to one-half of the same-gender estimate; the paper cites evidence that sibling spillovers and peer interactions are stronger within same-gender pairs (Dahl et al., 2024; Martin and Fabes, 2001).

formal.as_written: ρ^EO_CC = σ_γδA + σ_γδF + σ_γδM   (6')

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on families resident in Denmark 1980–2018 with both parents born 1935–1954 and the two first-born children born 1955–1973, and on children with at least five annual observations of the outcome over ages 31–45.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps are stated in Sections 2.1–2.2; the paper offers no assessment of how the conditioning affects the decomposition.

implies_edges.from: Family-quartet sample inclusion (two first-born children born 1955–1973; at least five annual outcome observations over ages 31–45)
implies_edges.to: Long-run disposable income of the child: average annual percentile rank over ages 31–45

key_assumptions.assumption: Each parent is assumed to have resided in their parish of birth until age 14, since addresses were only registered from 1968, so that distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school can be measured.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in footnote 11; no validation offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The comparison across parental access groups is interpreted as heterogeneity across parental educational-opportunity groups rather than as the causal effect of the 1937 school reform.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4.4 and repeated in the conclusion.

threats_discussed: Mixed-gender siblings may also share non-parental influences relevant for education–outcome gradients, in which case the baseline normalization attributes those influences to parental transmission, so parental transmission components are upper bounds

unresolved_confounders: Non-parental influences shared by mixed-gender siblings, which the baseline normalization attributes to parental transmission

estimator.value: Equally Weighted Minimum Distance (EWMD), matching observed correlations in education and economic outcomes to their model-implied counterparts; standard errors corrected post-estimation using the inverse sample variances of the moments

estimation.specification: Baseline latent-factor model of Equations (1)–(3) estimated separately on the access partition; the predicted own education–outcome gradient of Equation (7) is decomposed into its five components within the group.
estimation.weights: equally weighted moments (identity weighting matrix); no sampling weights

sample_n.value: Not printed: Table A3 reports no N. The 122,532 baseline families are split by whether the average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school is below or above the 60th percentile of all parental distances.

heterogeneity.dimension: parental access to middle schools: average parental distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school below (higher access) versus above (lower access) the 60th percentile
heterogeneity.finding: proportion of the predicted own education–disposable income gradient due to sibling-shared non-parental factors: higher-access families 0.05 (s.e. 0.02), lower-access families 0.08 (s.e. 0.02)
